years.headline: All-new power units, active aerodynamics and smaller cars reboot Formula 1.
keyChanges: Power split moves to roughly 50/50 between the combustion engine and the electric motor.
The MGU-H is removed and MGU-K electrical output nearly triples, from 120kW to 350kW.
Active aerodynamics arrive: front and rear wings switch between low-drag and high-downforce modes.
DRS is replaced by an electric 'Override' power boost for a car attacking the one ahead.
Cars are smaller and lighter: a shorter wheelbase, narrower bodywork and floor, and about 30kg less weight.
years.carDimensions: Narrower (around 100mm less) and lighter (around 30kg less) with a 200mm shorter maximum wheelbase of 3.4m and a narrower 1.9m floor. Ground-effect downforce is reduced by roughly 15-30% and overall drag is cut by up to around 40%.
years.powerUnit: The 1.6-litre V6 turbo is retained but with reduced combustion output. The complex MGU-H is gone and the MGU-K jumps from 120kW to 350kW for a roughly 50/50 power split, all running on fully sustainable fuel under a new energy-based fuel-flow limit.
years.aerodynamicRules: Formula 1's first full-time active aerodynamics: the front and rear wings move between a low-drag 'straight' mode and a high-downforce 'corner' mode. Ground-effect tunnels are reduced and overall drag is cut sharply to complement the new power units.
years.tyreRegulations: 18-inch Pirelli wheels are retained, but the front tyres are about 25mm narrower and the rears about 30mm narrower to save weight and reduce drag.
years.notableImpact: Billed by the FIA as the biggest technical change in the sport's history, arriving with a record six power-unit manufacturers, including Audi, a returning Honda and Red Bull Ford Powertrains, drawn in by the simpler hybrid concept.
funFacts: The 2026 MGU-K is almost three times more powerful than the 2025 version, jumping from 120kW to 350kW.
Removing the complex MGU-H helped attract a record six engine manufacturers, including Audi and Cadillac / General Motors.

visualComponents.label: Active aerodynamics
visualComponents.previousValue: Fixed wings with a DRS flap

years.headline: The last season before Formula 1's biggest-ever rule reset.
keyChanges: Final year of the 2022 ground-effect regulations before the 2026 reboot.
Tighter front- and rear-wing flexibility tests to stop flexing 'mini-DRS' wings.
A mandatory two-stop strategy was trialled at the Monaco Grand Prix.
Cooling allowances and minor safety updates.
years.carDimensions: Carried over from the ground-effect ruleset: a minimum weight of around 800kg with prescriptive bodywork around the underfloor tunnels.
years.powerUnit: 1.6-litre V6 turbo-hybrid in its final season, with groundwork laid for the 2026 switch to fully sustainable fuel.
years.aerodynamicRules: Clampdowns on flexing rear wings and bendy front wings, with the rest of the aero package stable ahead of 2026.
years.tyreRegulations: 18-inch Pirelli tyres, with Monaco running a one-off mandatory two-stop rule to liven up the race.
years.notableImpact: A transitional year as teams balanced winning in 2025 against preparing for the all-new 2026 rules.
funFacts: Monaco 2025 forced every driver to make at least two pit stops in an attempt to spice up a processional race.
2025 closed out the turbo-hybrid V6 era that had begun back in 2014.

years.headline: Fine-tuning the ground-effect cars before the 2026 revolution.
keyChanges: Largely stable regulations with minor aerodynamic and bodywork tweaks.
Clarifications on front-wing flexibility and additional cooling provisions.
DRS and bodywork refinements.
years.carDimensions: Unchanged ground-effect dimensions with a minimum weight of around 798kg.
years.powerUnit: 1.6-litre V6 turbo-hybrid under the ongoing development freeze, with teams beginning to split focus toward 2026.
years.aerodynamicRules: Stable ground-effect rules; teams converged on similar 'downwash' sidepod concepts as the design matured.
years.tyreRegulations: 18-inch Pirelli tyres with refined compound choices per event.
years.notableImpact: A closer competitive picture emerged as rivals caught the front-running team through the year.
funFacts: By 2024 most teams had converged on a similar downwash sidepod concept.
Teams increasingly diverted resources to their 2026 projects during the season.

years.headline: Floor edges raised to stamp out the bouncing that plagued 2022.
keyChanges: Floor edges and the diffuser throat raised to reduce porpoising and bouncing.
Stricter roll-hoop load tests after a high-profile 2022 crash.
Tweaks to diffuser and floor-edge regulations.
years.carDimensions: Ground-effect dimensions carried over, minimum weight around 798kg.
years.powerUnit: 1.6-litre V6 turbo-hybrid under the ongoing freeze.
years.aerodynamicRules: Floor edges lifted by 15mm and the diffuser throat raised to curb the violent bouncing of 2022.
years.tyreRegulations: 18-inch Pirelli tyres, with an alternative tyre allocation trialled at some events.
years.notableImpact: The leading team produced one of the most dominant seasons in history, winning all but one race.
funFacts: The 2023 season featured the most dominant constructor campaign in F1 history.
Roll-hoop tests were toughened after a dramatic 2022 Silverstone crash.

years.headline: Ground-effect cars return so drivers can race wheel-to-wheel again.
keyChanges: A ground-effect underfloor with Venturi tunnels replaces the flat floor.
Simplified over-wheel aerodynamics and a curled-over front wing and endplate.
18-inch wheels with low-profile Pirelli tyres replace the long-running 13-inch wheels.
Wheel covers and over-wheel winglets return; bargeboards are banned.
Minimum weight rises to a record of around 798kg.
years.carDimensions: The heaviest cars ever at around 798kg minimum, with standardised, prescriptive bodywork built around a ground-effect floor.
years.powerUnit: 1.6-litre V6 turbo-hybrid carried over under a development freeze, with a switch to E10 fuel (10% ethanol).
years.aerodynamicRules: Downforce is generated mainly by shaped underfloor tunnels rather than wings, cutting the turbulent wake so a following car keeps far more of its downforce, the change designed to enable closer racing. Early cars suffered violent 'porpoising' bouncing on the straights.
years.tyreRegulations: All-new 18-inch low-profile Pirelli tyres with stiffer sidewalls replace the 13-inch tyres used for decades.
years.notableImpact: A new front-runner emerged and dominated, while many cars suffered violent porpoising as their floors stalled at speed.
funFacts: Ground effect was last used in F1 in 1982 before being banned on safety grounds.
The 2022 cars were so prone to bouncing that the FIA introduced an anti-porpoising metric mid-season.

years.eraName: Hybrid Power Unit Era — Cost Cap
years.headline: A budget cap arrives and the floors are trimmed again.
keyChanges: The first-ever cost cap (around $145m) limits team spending.
Floor, diffuser and rear-brake-duct downforce cut by roughly 10%.
Aerodynamic testing restrictions scaled by championship position.
A power-unit development freeze is agreed to begin in 2022.
years.carDimensions: Wide-body dimensions carried over, minimum weight around 752kg.
years.powerUnit: 1.6-litre V6 turbo-hybrid, with a development freeze agreed to start the following year.
years.aerodynamicRules: A diagonal floor cut and smaller diffuser fences reduced downforce, hitting low-rake cars hardest.
years.tyreRegulations: Pirelli moved to a more robust tyre construction after failures the previous season.
years.notableImpact: The title was decided on the final lap of the final race in one of the most controversial deciders ever, in Abu Dhabi.
funFacts: The cost cap was F1's first serious attempt to level spending between the richest and poorest teams.
The 2021 championship was settled on the very last lap of the very last race amid huge controversy.

years.headline: A pandemic-hit season with minor floor cuts.
keyChanges: 2021 chassis development frozen due to COVID-19; the 2020 cars are largely carried over.
Floor, diffuser and brake-duct cuts reduce downforce for tyre safety.
Qualifying 'party modes' are banned from mid-season.
years.carDimensions: Wide-body dimensions carried over, minimum weight around 746kg.
years.powerUnit: 1.6-litre V6 turbo-hybrid, with engine modes effectively frozen during a race weekend from mid-season.
years.aerodynamicRules: Small floor cut-outs and diffuser changes reduced load on Pirelli's tyres after stresses the previous year.
years.tyreRegulations: Mostly the previous year's tyres re-used, with record-fast laps at Mugello and Monza.
years.notableImpact: A compressed 17-race calendar saw the leading driver equal Michael Schumacher's record of seven world titles.
funFacts: The 2020 season started in July and squeezed 17 races into the year after COVID delays.
Banning 'party mode' stopped teams cranking up engine power for a single qualifying lap.

years.headline: Simplified front wings aim to help cars follow more closely.
keyChanges: A wider, simpler front wing with fewer elements to cut outwash.
A larger, simpler rear wing with integrated DRS.
An extra 10kg minimum weight and more race fuel allowed (110kg).
Standardised biometric gloves for driver safety.
years.carDimensions: Wide-body dimensions carried over, minimum weight raised to around 743kg.
years.powerUnit: 1.6-litre V6 turbo-hybrid, with the race fuel allowance raised to 110kg.
years.aerodynamicRules: The front wing was widened and simplified, brake-duct winglets trimmed, and the rear wing enlarged to make following easier, a stop-gap before the 2022 overhaul.
years.tyreRegulations: Pirelli simplified its naming into a numbered C1-to-C5 range chosen per event.
years.notableImpact: Mercedes won the opening five races and cruised to another double title.
funFacts: Pirelli simplified its confusing compound names into a simple C1-to-C5 scale in 2019.
The 2019 aero tweaks were a preview of the close-racing philosophy behind the 2022 rules.

years.headline: The Halo cockpit-protection device becomes mandatory.
keyChanges: The Halo cockpit-protection structure is mandated on all cars.
Shark fins and rear T-wings are effectively banned.
A three-engine-per-season limit tightens reliability demands.
years.carDimensions: Wide-body dimensions, minimum weight raised to around 734kg to account for the Halo.
years.powerUnit: 1.6-litre V6 turbo-hybrid, with drivers limited to three power units for the season.
years.aerodynamicRules: Engine-cover shark fins and rear T-wings were outlawed; the Halo added a small new aerodynamic challenge.
years.tyreRegulations: Pirelli introduced hypersoft and superhard compounds, widening the range.
years.notableImpact: Mercedes fended off a strong Ferrari challenge, and the Halo was quickly vindicated in several crashes.
funFacts: The Halo is strong enough to support the weight of a London double-decker bus.
Many criticised the Halo's looks in 2018, but it has since saved several drivers' lives.

years.headline: Wider, faster, more aggressive cars deliver record lap times.
keyChanges: Cars are made wider: bodywork grows to 2000mm with wider front and rear wings.
Wider tyres (front +60mm, rear +80mm) for much more mechanical grip.
A larger diffuser and lower, swept-back rear wing for big downforce gains.
Minimum weight raised to accommodate the bigger cars.
years.carDimensions: Overall width back up to 2000mm from 1800mm, with a wider floor and diffuser and a minimum weight of 728kg.
years.powerUnit: 1.6-litre V6 turbo-hybrid, now more powerful and paired with far higher downforce.
years.aerodynamicRules: Wider bodywork, a bigger front wing, a lower and wider swept-back rear wing, and a larger diffuser produced roughly 25-30% more downforce and dramatically faster cornering.
years.tyreRegulations: Pirelli introduced significantly wider tyres to match the higher cornering loads.
years.notableImpact: Lap records tumbled and the cars looked more dramatic, though overtaking became harder in dirty air.
funFacts: The 2017 cars smashed pole-lap records that had stood since the V10 era.
The wider tyres offered roughly 25% more contact area than the 2016 rubber.

visualComponents.label: Bigger wing and diffuser
visualComponents.newValue: Larger wing and diffuser, about +30% downforce

years.headline: Engine tokens scrapped and radio coaching clamped down.
keyChanges: The power-unit token development system is abolished, freeing engine development.
Strict limits placed on pit-to-car radio coaching.
A brief and unpopular elimination-style qualifying format is trialled.
years.carDimensions: Narrow-body dimensions, minimum weight around 702kg.
years.powerUnit: 1.6-litre V6 turbo-hybrid, with development freer after the token system was dropped.
years.aerodynamicRules: Stable aerodynamics ahead of the big 2017 changes.
years.tyreRegulations: Pirelli expanded its compound range and let teams choose tyre allocations per race.
years.notableImpact: Nico Rosberg edged his team-mate to the title and then immediately retired from the sport.
funFacts: Rosberg retired just days after winning his only world championship.
The 2016 elimination-qualifying experiment was abandoned after only two races.

years.headline: Tighter nose rules tidy up the cars' looks.
keyChanges: Stricter nose-shape rules end the awkward 2014 'finger' noses.
The power-unit token development system continues.
The Virtual Safety Car is introduced.
years.carDimensions: Narrow-body dimensions, minimum weight around 702kg.
years.powerUnit: 1.6-litre V6 turbo-hybrid developed within a 'token' system that limited changes.
years.aerodynamicRules: Reworked nose regulations for safety and aesthetics.
years.tyreRegulations: Pirelli control tyres with compound choices made per event.
years.notableImpact: Mercedes and Lewis Hamilton dominated again, with the rest of the field chasing the silver cars.
funFacts: The Virtual Safety Car was introduced after the 2014 Japanese Grand Prix tragedy.
Engine upgrades were rationed via a 'token' system that limited what could change.

years.headline: Turbo-hybrid V6 power units usher in F1's most complex engines ever.
keyChanges: 1.6-litre V6 turbo-hybrid power units replace the 2.4-litre V8s.
Energy recovery via MGU-K and MGU-H feeds a battery for deployment.
Fuel is limited to 100kg per race with a 100kg/hr fuel-flow cap.
Eight-speed gearboxes are mandated and the minimum weight is raised.
A lower, narrower front wing and a single exhaust outlet.
years.carDimensions: Minimum weight raised to 691kg, with lower noses for safety and the front wing narrowed to 1650mm.
years.powerUnit: A 1.6-litre V6 single-turbo hybrid combining a combustion engine with MGU-K (kinetic) and MGU-H (heat) recovery, around 600 bhp from the engine plus roughly 160 bhp of electrical power, all under tight fuel limits.
years.aerodynamicRules: Lower nose tips (producing some awkward shapes), a narrower front wing, and a single tailpipe that ended exhaust-blown aerodynamics.
years.tyreRegulations: Pirelli tyres were tuned for the heavier, torquier hybrid cars.
years.notableImpact: Mercedes began a period of total dominance, with Hamilton and Rosberg fighting for the title.
funFacts: The 2014 power units recover energy from both braking and exhaust heat.
These hybrids became the most efficient racing engines ever, exceeding 50% thermal efficiency.

years.headline: The last hurrah for the V8s before the hybrid revolution.
keyChanges: DRS use is restricted to designated zones in practice and qualifying too.
Tyre construction is revised mid-season after a string of failures.
The final season of the 2.4-litre V8 formula.
years.carDimensions: Narrow-body dimensions, minimum weight 642kg.
years.powerUnit: 2.4-litre V8 with KERS in its final season before hybrids.
years.aerodynamicRules: Coanda-effect exhausts were refined, and DRS was now limited to race zones in all sessions.
years.tyreRegulations: Pirelli switched tyre construction mid-season after high-profile blowouts at Silverstone.
years.notableImpact: The leading driver won 13 races, including nine in a row, to claim a fourth consecutive title.
funFacts: The champion won the final nine races of 2013 in succession.
2013 closed the book on naturally aspirated engines that had run since 1989.

years.headline: Stepped 'platypus' noses appear under new height rules.
keyChanges: Lower nose-height rules produce distinctive stepped noses.
Exhaust position is standardised to curb blown-diffuser effects.
The minimum weight is raised slightly.
years.carDimensions: Narrow-body dimensions, minimum weight 640kg.
years.powerUnit: 2.4-litre V8 with KERS.
years.aerodynamicRules: Mandated lower chassis fronts forced ugly stepped noses, and exhaust outlets were relocated to reduce aerodynamic blowing of the diffuser.
years.tyreRegulations: Pirelli high-degradation tyres produced an unusually unpredictable first half of the season.
years.notableImpact: The title was decided by three points in a dramatic, rain-hit finale in Brazil.
funFacts: The first seven races of 2012 produced seven different winners.
The stepped-nose rule was about safety, but teams disliked how it looked.

years.headline: DRS and Pirelli's high-degradation tyres transform the racing.
keyChanges: The Drag Reduction System (DRS) is introduced to aid overtaking.
Pirelli replaces Bridgestone as sole supplier with deliberately high-degradation tyres.
KERS returns across the grid.
The 107% qualifying rule is reinstated.
years.carDimensions: Narrow-body dimensions, minimum weight 640kg.
years.powerUnit: 2.4-litre V8 with KERS now standard equipment.
years.aerodynamicRules: The movable rear-wing DRS was allowed freely in practice and qualifying and within zones in the race; off-throttle blown diffusers were restricted mid-season.
years.tyreRegulations: Pirelli introduced tyres designed to degrade quickly, forcing multiple pit stops and varied strategy.
years.notableImpact: Red Bull and Sebastian Vettel dominated, but races became far more action-packed.
funFacts: Pirelli was specifically asked to build fast-degrading tyres to make races less predictable.
DRS could be used anywhere on the lap in qualifying in its first season.

years.headline: In-race refuelling is banned, putting strategy on tyres alone.
keyChanges: Refuelling during races is banned; cars must start with full fuel.
Narrower front tyres to rebalance the heavier cars.
KERS is dropped by the teams for the season by agreement.
A new points system (25-18-15-12-10-8-6-4-2-1) for a larger grid.
years.carDimensions: Narrow-body dimensions, minimum weight 620kg.
years.powerUnit: 2.4-litre V8; teams ran without KERS this year by agreement.
years.aerodynamicRules: F-duct stalled-rear-wing systems and blown diffusers became the development battlegrounds.
years.tyreRegulations: Bridgestone's final season, with narrower front tyres to balance cars now carrying full fuel loads.
years.notableImpact: Sebastian Vettel became F1's youngest champion in a four-way title decider in Abu Dhabi.
funFacts: Banning refuelling meant cars started races carrying over 150kg of fuel.
Four drivers could still mathematically win the title at the 2010 season finale.

years.headline: A radical aero reset, the return of slick tyres, and KERS hybrid boost.
keyChanges: A major aero overhaul: a wide, low front wing and a tall, narrow rear wing.
Slick tyres return after eleven years of grooved tyres.
KERS (Kinetic Energy Recovery System) is introduced as an optional hybrid boost.
Bargeboards and most aero appendages are banned to cut turbulent wake.
A driver-adjustable front-wing flap is permitted.
years.carDimensions: Front wing widened to around 1800mm and lowered; rear wing made taller and narrower at around 750mm wide; minimum weight 605kg.
years.powerUnit: 2.4-litre V8 plus optional KERS giving around 80 bhp of boost for roughly 6.6 seconds per lap.
years.aerodynamicRules: The front wing was widened and lowered, the rear wing raised and narrowed, and dozens of small aero devices banned to reduce 'dirty air' and aid overtaking. The double-diffuser loophole defined the season.
years.tyreRegulations: Slick tyres returned for the first time since 1997, increasing mechanical grip, with Bridgestone the sole supplier.
years.notableImpact: Brawn GP, born from the ashes of Honda, won both titles in a fairytale debut season by exploiting the double diffuser.
funFacts: Brawn GP entered as a brand-new team and won both championships in its only full season.
KERS was optional in 2009, and several front-running teams chose not to run it at first.

visualComponents.label: Wide low front wing
visualComponents.newValue: Wider and lower to the ground

years.headline: A standard ECU arrives and traction control is banned for good.
keyChanges: A single standardised electronic control unit (ECU) is mandated.
Traction control and engine-braking aids are banned again.
Gearboxes must last four consecutive events.
years.carDimensions: Narrow-body dimensions, minimum weight 605kg.
years.powerUnit: 2.4-litre V8 under a development freeze, with driver aids stripped away by the standard ECU.
years.aerodynamicRules: The last year of the highly developed, appendage-heavy aero before the 2009 overhaul.
years.tyreRegulations: Bridgestone grooved control tyres with two compounds per weekend.
years.notableImpact: Lewis Hamilton won his first title at the final corner of the final lap in Brazil.
funFacts: The standardised ECU finally removed traction control by making it technically impossible to run.
Hamilton clinched the 2008 title with a last-corner overtake on the final lap.

years.headline: Bridgestone becomes the sole tyre supplier.
keyChanges: A single tyre supplier (Bridgestone) for the whole grid.
An engine development freeze begins to control costs.
Both dry compounds must be used during a race.
years.carDimensions: Narrow-body dimensions, minimum weight 605kg.
years.powerUnit: 2.4-litre V8 under a development freeze, producing around 750 bhp.
years.aerodynamicRules: Aero remained free, and teams developed intricate flick-ups and bridge wings.
years.tyreRegulations: Bridgestone control tyres with two dry compounds per weekend, both of which had to be used; the softer was marked with a white sidewall groove.
years.notableImpact: Kimi Raikkonen won the title for Ferrari by a single point in a three-way finale.
funFacts: The 2007 title was decided by just one point between three drivers going into the finale.
With one tyre supplier, a white sidewall marking was introduced to identify the softer compound.

years.headline: 2.4-litre V8 engines replace the screaming V10s.
keyChanges: Engines switch from the 3.0L V10 to a 2.4L V8 to cut power and cost.
Tyre changes during races are permitted again.
Mass-damper devices are banned mid-season.
A knockout qualifying format is introduced.
years.carDimensions: Narrow-body dimensions, minimum weight 600kg.
years.powerUnit: A new 2.4-litre naturally aspirated V8 producing around 750 bhp at up to roughly 20,000 rpm. Smaller teams could run a rev-limited V10 for one more year.
years.aerodynamicRules: The mass-damper device used by Renault was banned by the FIA mid-season; aero was otherwise stable.
years.tyreRegulations: Tyre changes were allowed again, ending the 2005 single-set rule, in the final season of the Bridgestone-Michelin war.
years.notableImpact: Fernando Alonso beat Michael Schumacher to a second title in Schumacher's first farewell season.
funFacts: 2006 was the last season of the Bridgestone-Michelin tyre war before a single supplier took over.
Renault's banned 'mass damper' was a tuned weight that smoothed the car over bumps.

years.headline: No tyre changes and two-race engines force a rethink of durability.
keyChanges: Tyres must last the entire race, with no changes except for safety or wet conditions.
One engine must last two race weekends.
An aero cut: the front wing is raised, the rear wing moved forward, and the diffuser revised to reduce downforce.
An aggregate-qualifying format is trialled, then dropped mid-season.
years.carDimensions: Narrow-body dimensions with aero surfaces cut to slow the cars; minimum weight 605kg.
years.powerUnit: 3.0-litre V10 in its final season, now needing to last two weekends, a major reliability challenge.
years.aerodynamicRules: The front wing was raised by 50mm, the rear wing brought forward, and the rear diffuser height reduced, a deliberate downforce cut for safety.
years.tyreRegulations: A single set of tyres for qualifying and the full race distance dramatically changed strategy and rewarded tyre management; it led to the controversial US Grand Prix where the Michelin runners withdrew.
years.notableImpact: Renault's Fernando Alonso ended Ferrari's run to become F1's youngest champion at the time, while the US GP saw only six cars start.
funFacts: At the 2005 US Grand Prix only six cars raced after the Michelin teams withdrew over tyre safety.
The no-tyre-change rule made tyre management a defining driver skill for the season.

years.headline: One engine must now last an entire race weekend.
keyChanges: Engines must survive a full race weekend or incur a ten-place grid penalty.
Aerodynamic tweaks to the rear wing and winglets.
Mid-season clampdown on extra aero appendages.
years.carDimensions: Narrow-body dimensions, minimum weight 605kg.
years.powerUnit: 3.0-litre V10 with a new one-engine-per-weekend durability rule, with outputs near 900 bhp.
years.aerodynamicRules: Limits on the number of winglets, with a mid-season clampdown on extra aero appendages.
years.tyreRegulations: The Bridgestone-Michelin war at its peak, with Ferrari and Bridgestone dominant.
years.notableImpact: Michael Schumacher won 13 of 18 races and a seventh world title.
funFacts: 2004 set a record with 13 wins for one driver in a single season.
The one-engine-per-weekend rule was F1's first real step toward engine-life limits.

years.headline: A new points system and single-lap qualifying are introduced to spice up the show.
keyChanges: Points are awarded to the top eight (10-8-6-5-4-3-2-1) instead of the top six.
Single-car, one-lap qualifying replaces the old twelve-lap session.
Parc ferme rules lock car setup between qualifying and the race.
Spare-car usage during sessions is heavily restricted.
years.carDimensions: Narrow-body dimensions, minimum weight 600kg (largely unchanged).
years.powerUnit: 3.0-litre V10, with engines still changeable between sessions.
years.aerodynamicRules: Aero remained free as teams chased qualifying-specific low-fuel setups under the new format.
years.tyreRegulations: The tyre war continued, with qualifying now run on race-fuel loads, changing tyre strategy.
years.notableImpact: The closer points spread kept the title race alive late, with Schumacher beating Raikkonen by two points.
funFacts: The 2003 points change was the first major overhaul of F1 scoring since 1991.
Single-lap qualifying meant one mistake could ruin a driver's entire weekend.

years.headline: Ferrari's F2002 delivers one of the most dominant seasons in F1 history.
keyChanges: Regulations were largely stable, with refinement of the electronic driver aids.
Continued tyre-war development between Bridgestone and Michelin.
Increasingly sophisticated traction and launch control.
years.carDimensions: Narrow-body dimensions, minimum weight 600kg.
years.powerUnit: 3.0-litre V10, with outputs climbing past 850 bhp.
years.aerodynamicRules: Free aero development, with teams pushing slim 'coke-bottle' rear bodywork.
years.tyreRegulations: The Bridgestone-Michelin development war intensified.
years.notableImpact: Ferrari won 15 of 17 races, and Schumacher finished every race on the podium.
funFacts: Schumacher scored a podium in every single race of the 2002 season.
Ferrari secured the constructors' title by July, the earliest ever at the time.

years.headline: Traction control and launch control return mid-season after proving impossible to police.
keyChanges: Traction control is re-legalised from the Spanish Grand Prix (round 5) onwards.
Launch control and fully automatic gearboxes are permitted again.
Beryllium alloys are banned in engines and other components.
Greater focus on electronic engine management.
years.carDimensions: Unchanged from 2000: narrow-body dimensions, minimum weight 600kg.
years.powerUnit: 3.0-litre V10s, now paired with sophisticated electronic engine and traction-management software.
years.aerodynamicRules: Aero development continued freely, with bargeboards and high noses refined.
years.tyreRegulations: Michelin returned to F1 as a tyre supplier, reigniting the Bridgestone-Michelin tyre war and rapid compound development.
years.notableImpact: The FIA conceded it could not reliably detect illegal traction control, so re-legalised it, a rare reversal that reshaped car electronics.
funFacts: The FIA u-turn on traction control happened because policing software-based launch control had become technically impossible.
Michael Schumacher clinched the title with four races to spare, the earliest in F1 history at the time.

years.headline: The 3.0L V10 grooved-tyre formula matures as Ferrari's dominance begins.
keyChanges: Naturally aspirated 3.0-litre V10 engines, free-revving with no rev limit.
Four longitudinal grooves required on both front and rear dry tyres.
Electronic driver aids such as traction and launch control remained banned.
Cockpit side-impact protection requirements strengthened for driver safety.
years.carDimensions: Maximum width 1800mm and minimum weight 600kg including the driver, on the narrow-track chassis introduced in 1998.
years.powerUnit: A naturally aspirated 3.0-litre V10 revving to around 17,000-18,000 rpm and producing roughly 800 bhp, with no engine-life limits, so fresh engines every session were common.
years.aerodynamicRules: Front and rear wings were largely free within box dimensions, and high-nose concepts and complex bargeboards developed turbulent but powerful aero.
years.tyreRegulations: Grooved dry tyres (four grooves front and rear) had been mandated since 1998 to cut cornering speeds, with Bridgestone the sole supplier this season.
years.notableImpact: Michael Schumacher won Ferrari's first drivers' title since 1979, starting an era of red dominance.
funFacts: Engines of this era could rev beyond 17,000 rpm and were rebuilt after almost every session.
Ferrari had not won a drivers' championship for 21 years before Schumacher's 2000 title.
